1586: Starch content is contingent upon the efficiency with which assimilate was translocated into the endosperm during grain filling. In the prepared product it is further modified by the loss of low-molecular-weight material and by the water imbibed during cooking. Earlier work is concordant: Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) noted that starch constitutes approximately nine tenths of milled rice on a dry weight basis, and Tian et al. (2018) concluded that the residual starch is swollen and less crystalline. Iqbal et al. (2021) demonstrated that restructured starch resists digestion, and Cheng et al. (2019) established that the extent of starch gelatinisation governs texture and digestibility.
1587: The leading cultivar varied with the product, Kalonunia, Kataribhog, Lal Badshabhog and Radhunipagal ranking highest in turn, so that no single recommendation covers the group on this attribute.
1594: Protein constitutes the principal nutritional contribution of rice after energy and additionally firms the cooked grain through disulphide bonding. For table rice the values lay between 2.56 and 3.36%, with the control at 2.56%; 3 of the cultivars exceeded the control, Radhunipagal ranking highest. In khichdi the values ranged from 16.49 in Kalojira to 18.23% in Gobindabhog; the control recorded 16.74%, no cultivar exceeded the control, and Gobindabhog returned the most favourable value. Kalojira recorded the highest value in pulao at 4.35% and Dudeshwar the lowest at 3.62%, the control recording 3.62%; 2 cultivars exceeded it and Kalojira ranked most favourable. For payash the values lay between 5.39 and 6.57%, with the control at 5.39%; here one cultivar exceeded the control and Kalonunia ranked highest. The values appear in Table 4.42, with Fig. 4.7 presenting the same data.
1595: Only 3 of the 4 products exhibited a significant cultivar effect. Year and its interaction with cultivar both fell short of significance, so that the order was identical in each year. Variation between replicates was small, the coefficient of variation lying between 6.60 and 8.64%. The greater part of the protein is glutelin sequestered in protein bodies beneath the aleurone, and the quantity is contingent upon the nitrogen translocated into the grain during filling. Cooking does not alter it.
1596: Published work is concordant. Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) reported that total protein is unaltered by hydrothermal treatment; Cheng et al. (2019) observed that disulphide cross-links elevate firmness; and Akter et al. (2025) recorded that protein rose from 6.68 to 9.42% following treatment, while Iqbal et al. (2021) determined that the protein network governs enzyme access to starch. The leading position was shared between Gobindabhog, Kalojira, Kalonunia and Radhunipagal, so that selection on this attribute must be made product by product.
1603: Soluble protein is the fraction remaining extractable, and therefore digestible, after cooking; a higher value indicates that heat has not aggregated the protein. In table rice the values ranged from 0.47 in Dudeshwar to 0.61% in Radhunipagal; with the control at 0.47%, 6 cultivars exceeded it and Radhunipagal proved the best. Gobindabhog recorded the highest value in khichdi at 1.64% and Dudeshwar the lowest at 1.37%; against 1.37% for the control, 8 cultivars exceeded it, Gobindabhog being the most favourable entry. For pulao the values lay between 0.53 and 0.90%, with the control at 0.53%; 9 cultivars exceeded the control, Tulaipanji ranking highest among them. In payash the values ranged from 1.19 in Lal Badshabhog to 1.56% in Gobindabhog; the control recorded 1.31%, 6 cultivars exceeded it, and Gobindabhog proved the most favourable. Means for this attribute are set out in Table 4.43 and illustrated in Fig. 4.8. All the products exhibited a significant cultivar effect. Neither year nor the year × cultivar term attained significance, ranking being unchanged between years. With coefficients of variation of 1.32 to 3.62%, the experiment was well controlled.
1604: Heat ruptures the protein bodies and subsequently cross-links the liberated chains through disulphide bonds, thereby reducing the extractable fraction; cultivars richer in cysteine forfeit more. The same pattern has been reported previously. Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) demonstrated that solubility alters while total protein does not, and Cheng et al. (2019) noted that cross-linking reduces the extractable fraction. Kabir et al. (2025) concluded that treatment modifies the association between protein and bound phenolics, and Roy et al. (2019) demonstrated that solubility declines as steaming and soaking become more severe.
1605: Gobindabhog, Radhunipagal and Tulaipanji each headed the ranking in a different product, so that this attribute cannot determine the selection for the group as a whole.
1612: Lipid is localised in the germ and aleurone and carries the fat-soluble vitamins and the aroma compounds. A higher content is preferable, although excess lipid curtails shelf life. Radhunipagal recorded the highest value in table rice at 0.34% and Gobindabhog the lowest at 0.23%; against 0.32% for the control, no cultivar exceeded the control, and Radhunipagal was the most favourable entry. For khichdi the values lay between 10.78 and 13.25%, with the control at 13.25%; here no cultivar exceeded the control and Dudeshwar ranked highest. In pulao the values ranged from 3.06 in Gobindabhog to 3.53% in Kalojira; the control recorded 3.49%, no cultivar exceeded the control, and Kalojira returned the most favourable value. Dudeshwar recorded the highest value in payash at 7.06% and Gobindabhog the lowest at 6.70%; against 7.06% for the control, no cultivar exceeded the control, and Dudeshwar was the most favourable entry. Table 4.44 carries the means, which are plotted in Fig. 4.9.
1613: The cultivar effect was significant in 2 products out of 4. Year was significant in 1 products and the year × cultivar interaction in 1; the order of the cultivars therefore being largely stable. The coefficient of variation remained within 2.62 to 11.44%, indicative of good precision. Lipid is stored as triacylglycerol in the germ and aleurone, so the value reflects both the extent of these tissues in the cultivar and the degree of milling.
1614: Earlier reports corroborate this finding. Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) determined that lipid resides in the germ and aleurone and oxidises readily, and Hu et al. (2019) reported that the movement of water within the kernel displaces the lipid-bearing tissues. Devi and Badwaik (2022) observed that traditional cultivars differ widely in proximate composition, and Oliveira et al. (2026) recorded that milling is the principal route by which the outer layers are lost. No single cultivar proved superior across all the products: Dudeshwar, Kalojira and Radhunipagal ranked highest in different ones, so that the decision is contingent upon the product concerned.
1621: Ash is the residue remaining after ignition and represents the total inorganic contribution of the grain. For table rice the values lay between 0.13 and 0.43%, with the control at 0.43%; here no cultivar exceeded the control and Dudeshwar ranked highest. In khichdi the values ranged from 1.94 in Radhatilak to 2.39% in Dudeshwar; the control recorded 2.39%, no cultivar exceeded the control, and Dudeshwar returned the most favourable value. Dudeshwar recorded the highest value in pulao at 1.08% and Gobindabhog the lowest at 0.81%; against 1.08% for the control, no cultivar exceeded the control, and Dudeshwar was the most favourable entry. For payash the values lay between 1.24 and 1.60%, with the control at 1.60%; here no cultivar exceeded the control and Dudeshwar ranked highest. The data are presented in Table 4.45 and plotted in Fig. 4.10. The cultivars separated significantly wherever the attribute was determined. The year effect was non-significant in every product, though the year × cultivar interaction was significant in 2, so that in those products the differences between cultivars were not of equal magnitude in both years. Precision was satisfactory, coefficients of variation ranging from 0.75 to 7.17%.
1622: Ash follows the germ and aleurone, which carry the greater part of the mineral matter, so that cultivars with a thicker aleurone or a larger embryo return higher values. Comparable results have been published elsewhere. Hu et al. (2019) demonstrated that ash follows the proportion of germ and aleurone surviving, and Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) noted that the spread in ash derives from the outer grain layers. Jannasch and Wang (2020) concluded that the steeping medium may augment the mineral fraction, and Kumar et al. (2022) demonstrated that ash is redistributed rather than lost on treatment.
1623: Dudeshwar returned the most favourable value in every product of this group and is therefore the cultivar to select where a high value is required.
1631: Phenolic acids are the principal antioxidants of the grain and are largely bound to the pericarp cell wall; a higher retained content in the product is preferable. In table rice the values ranged from 0.30 in Dudeshwar to 0.55 mg GAE/g in Kalonunia; the control recorded 0.30 mg GAE/g, 9 cultivars exceeded the control, and Kalonunia returned the most favourable value. Lal Badshabhog recorded the highest value in khichdi at 6.44 mg GAE/g and Radhatilak the lowest at 5.19 mg GAE/g; against 5.23 mg GAE/g for the control, 8 cultivars exceeded the control, Lal Badshabhog being the most favourable entry. For pulao the values lay between 1.69 and 3.66 mg GAE/g, with the control at 2.57 mg GAE/g; 3 cultivars exceeded the control and Kataribhog ranked first. In payash the values ranged from 10.16 in Radhunipagal to 52.32 mg GAE/g in Kalonunia; the control recorded 10.98 mg GAE/g, 8 cultivars exceeded the control, and Kalonunia returned the most favourable value. Table 4.46 lists the means and Fig. 4.11 presents them graphically.
1632: Cultivars differed significantly in all the products. Significance attached to year in 3 products and to the year × cultivar interaction in 3, leaving cultivar ranking broadly unchanged from year to year. Coefficients of variation lay between 0.47 and 3.59%, attesting to the precision of the trial. The greater part of the phenolic acid is bound to arabinoxylan in the pericarp wall. Heat cleaves these bonds and liberates it while concurrently degrading and leaching the free fraction, so that the value recorded represents the balance of the two processes.
1633: Comparable observations appear in the literature. Phimphilai et al. (2026) determined that popping and steam cooking reduce total phenolics markedly, and Shavandi et al. (2023) reported that infrared puffing elevates the extractable fraction. Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) observed that heat liberates ferulic and p-coumaric acid from the cell wall, and Kabir et al. (2025) recorded that soaking and cooking reduce phenolic acids, the bound fraction exceeding the free. The leading cultivar varied with the product, Kalonunia, Kataribhog and Lal Badshabhog ranking highest in turn, so that no single recommendation covers the group on this attribute.
1640: Flavonoids contribute to antioxidant activity and to pericarp colour. They degrade readily on heating, so that the residual content indicates the gentleness of the treatment applied. Gobindabhog recorded the highest value in khichdi at 0.04 mg QE/g and Dudeshwar the lowest at 0.03 mg QE/g; against 0.03 mg QE/g for the control, 7 cultivars exceeded the control, Gobindabhog being the most favourable entry. For pulao the values lay between 1.43 and 2.53 mg QE/g, with the control at 1.81 mg QE/g; here 6 cultivars exceeded the control, Kataribhog ranking highest. In payash the values ranged from 5.20 in Dudeshwar to 22.54 mg QE/g in Kalonunia; the control recorded 5.20 mg QE/g, 9 cultivars exceeded the control, and Kalonunia returned the most favourable value. The means are given in Table 4.47 and plotted in Fig. 4.12. The cultivars differed significantly in every product. In 3 products the year effect was significant and in 3 the year × cultivar interaction, the cultivars thus retaining a similar order in both years. The coefficient of variation ranged from 0.68 to 2.36%, indicating reliable measurement.
1641: Flavonoids are synthesised in the pericarp, and cultivars differ in the quantity deposited. They are readily destroyed by heat, so that the residual content reflects both the initial level and the treatment applied. Previous studies describe the same behaviour. Phimphilai et al. (2026) demonstrated that flavonoids degrade more readily than total phenolics, and Kabir et al. (2025) noted that most flavonoid resides in the bound fraction. Oliveira et al. (2026) concluded that protracted cooking may incur losses of up to forty per cent, and Devi and Badwaik (2022) demonstrated that traditional cultivars differ several fold.
1642: The leading position was shared between Gobindabhog, Kalonunia and Kataribhog, so that selection on this attribute must be made product by product.
1649: Antioxidant capacity measures the activity of the entire bioactive fraction rather than its quantity, so that a higher value is desirable. For table rice the values lay between 7.20 and 8.21 mg TE/g, with the control at 7.20 mg TE/g; Lal Badshabhog ranked first, and 6 cultivars in all exceeded the control. In khichdi the values ranged from 21.84 in Kalojira to 23.98 mg TE/g in Radhunipagal; the control recorded 23.00 mg TE/g, 4 cultivars exceeded the control, and Radhunipagal returned the most favourable value. Kataribhog recorded the highest value in pulao at 9.69 mg TE/g and Dudeshwar the lowest at 7.63 mg TE/g; against 7.63 mg TE/g for the control, 9 cultivars exceeded the control, Kataribhog being the most favourable entry. For payash the values lay between 10.11 and 13.84 mg TE/g, with the control at 10.11 mg TE/g; 9 of the cultivars exceeded the control, Kalonunia ranking highest. Table 4.48 gives the means and Fig. 4.13 presents them.
